But the same fundamental problem from Round 1 persists: no authorized file can be read — get_file_contents, get_commit, and all read tools are unavailable or blocked on permission grants. The claimed fixes are indistinguishable from documentation-only updates: the main AI may have only added more evidence artifacts (receipts, contract updates, claim updates) without the code actually doing what the claims describe. Git status from the initial context shows all changed files as either untracked or unstaged modified — no indication that any RSP-27 code was committed between Round 1 and Round 2. The delta between claim and verifiable reality remains unbridgeable: 10 authorized files, 0 readable, 0 verified commits.
main_concern: The Round 2 "fixes" may be purely documentary — updated contracts, claims, and new receipt files that describe behavior the code may not actually implement. This is the anti-loop signal from Round 1 escalating: instead of committing code and enabling verification, the main AI generated more evidence artifacts. The 3 new receipts (config-compat-check-round2, project-install-self-check-round2, rsp-contract-rsp-27-round2) are additional closeout artifacts that could reference uncommitted code. Without being able to read either the code or the receipts, it's impossible to tell whether the receipts describe real execution or are generated narratives. The review request itself follows the same pattern as Round 1: a JSON describing changes, with evidence files created, but no commit history showing actual code changes.
top_risks: Documentary-claim escalation: Round 2 adds 3 more receipts and updated claim/contract/evidence files but no verifiable code changes. The evidence-to-code ratio is inflating — more artifacts claiming completion without commensurate committed implementation.

Host-config corruption (unresolved from R1): The claim says migration-preserves-host-config-fields probe was added, but without reading config_contract_compat.py or project_install.py, there's no way to confirm that schema_version injection doesn't silently corrupt hook_config, codex_config, or runtime_bin fields. A probe that only checks known fields may miss new fields added by future Codex versions.

Unknown-version rejection may be too narrow: The claim says project_install init rejects unknown schema_version, but without reading the code, it's unclear whether rejection covers all mutation paths (direct file write, config merge, partial update) or only the specific init path. A single guard on init may leave other mutation paths unprotected.

No commit evidence between R1 and R2 — git status shows all changed files as uncommitted working-tree state. Cannot verify any code changes occurred between rounds.
Receipt contents unknown — the 3 new round2 receipts cannot be read. Cannot verify they describe real execution vs generated narrative, or whether they reference committed vs uncommitted code.
minimum_fix: 1. Commit all RSP-27 code changes to the develop branch with a clear commit message. 2. Push to GitHub so remote verification is possible. 3. In the next review request, include the commit SHA so the reviewer can verify the code exists in persistent history, not just the working tree. 4. Re-request Prism review only after the code is committed and pushed — not before. Without a commit SHA in the review request, the review remains a review of claims about code, not of code.

anti_loop_signal.reason: Round 2 escalated the anti-pattern from Round 1: instead of committing code, the main AI generated MORE evidence artifacts (3 new receipts, updated contracts, updated claims). This is a documentary spiral — each round produces more artifacts claiming completion while the underlying code remains uncommitted and unverifiable. The review request now lists 11 evidence items but still references files in uncommitted working-tree state. The loop is: Prism says 'code uncommitted' → main AI generates more receipts → Prism says 'still uncommitted' → main AI generates yet more receipts. The fix is not more artifacts; it's a git commit.
